title: Map Reading
tagline: Conventional signs, directions, scale, grid references and contour interpretation, with the map work assessment

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ICSE Class IX Geography unit 'Map Work'. The unit is part of the 30-mark internal assessment: the record file of map exercises carries 10 marks and the project report carries 10 marks, and the syllabus does not print the breakdown of the remaining 10 marks. The record file exercises listed in the syllabus are the uses of the important types of maps, the directions and how to identify them, the reading and use of the statement of scale, the graphic scale and the representative fraction, the reading of a town guide map or an atlas map with the recognition of the symbols and colours and the identification of directions and distances, the drawing and recognition of the forms of the important contours, and the drawing of at least one sketch map. Every exercise in the assessment section of this chapter is a self-contained textual or tabular exercise, because the platform has no map-image component; no map image, coordinate, legend or source-specific data has been invented, and each question is answerable from the exercise data given with it. No board examination paper was consulted, so every practice question is original and not a previous year question.

learningOutcomes: Recognise the conventional signs and the colours used on a topographical or town guide map.
Give and read the cardinal, intercardinal and three-figure bearing directions of a map.
Convert between a representative fraction, a statement of scale and a graphic scale, and measure distance with each of them.
Give the four-figure grid reference of a point on a map and use the national grid.
Identify the landforms shown by contour patterns and state the contour interval.
Interpret the pattern of settlement, roads and drainage on a map.
Complete the map work exercises of the record file with a clear answer key.

overview.intro: A map is a drawing of a part of the earth's surface on a flat sheet, and it is read by its conventions: the symbols and colours of the key, the direction that north lies in, the scale that turns a measured distance into a real distance, the grid that fixes the position of a place, and the contour lines that show the shape of the land. This chapter takes up those conventions in turn and then applies them in the map work section. The earlier chapter on Maps and Their Uses sets out how maps are classified; here the emphasis is on reading one. The scale of a topographical sheet, the reading of a town guide map, the recognition of the forms of the important contours and the sketch map are the exercises that the internal assessment asks for, and each of the six exercises in the assessment section below is set out with the data it needs and with an answer key that explains how the answer is arrived at.

facts.value: Symbols and colours, direction, scale, position on the grid, and relief from the contours

facts.label: Colours on a topographical sheet
facts.value: Blue for water, green for vegetation, brown for contours and relief, black for buildings, yellow for roads

blocks.text: A conventional sign is a symbol that has been agreed upon and used on every map of a country to show a particular feature, so that a reader can identify it at once without a key. The key, or legend, of a map is the panel that lists these symbols with their meanings. The signs are chosen so that the feature is suggested by the drawing itself: a railway line is drawn as a line with short bars across it like the sleepers of a track, a bridge is drawn as two short parallel lines across the road or the stream, a church is shown by a cross, a mosque by a small dome with a minaret, a lighthouse by a tower with rays drawn from the top, and a benchmark by a small circle with a dot at the centre. Colour is used in the same way. On a topographical sheet blue marks the water, green marks the vegetation, brown marks the contours and the relief, black is used for the buildings and for the lettering, and yellow is used for the roads, with a red band for the trunk roads and a white band for the metalled roads. Red is also used for the towns and the built-up area on a political map.

rows: Rivers, streams, canals, tanks, lakes and the sea
Forests, scrub, orchards and the wooded country
Contour lines, the height of the land, roads in cutting and embankments

items: A benchmark is a permanent mark of a known height above mean sea level, and the number beside it gives the height in metres.
The conventional sign of a survey of India with a number shows the height of a spot above mean sea level.
An embankment is drawn as a bank with the slope on one side only, and a cutting as a bank with the slope on both sides.
A metalled road is a road surfaced with stone or tar, and an unmetalled road and a cart track are drawn differently on the map.
The key of a map must always be read first, because the meaning of a symbol can differ from one map to another.

blocks.text: On an ordinary map the north is at the top of the sheet, the east is to the right, the south at the bottom and the west to the left, and this is called the orientation of the map. The four cardinal points are north, south, east and west, and between them lie the four intercardinal points, the north-east, the south-east, the south-west and the north-west. All eight together make the eight points of the compass. A finer set of sixteen points is used when a direction has to be given more exactly, and the direction of the sixteen points is named in the same way, for example north-north-east. For map work the direction is usually written as a bearing, a number of degrees measured clockwise from north. North is 000 degrees, east is 090 degrees, south is 180 degrees and west is 270 degrees, and the north-east is 045 degrees. The three-figure bearing of a line is always given from the point of observation to the point named, so the bearing of a place from another place and the bearing of the second place from the first differ by 180 degrees.

items.meaning: The setting out of the map, with north at the top, east to the right, south at the bottom and west to the left.
The direction of a line measured clockwise from north and written as a number of degrees, from 000 to 360.
The direction of the earth's magnetic field, which differs slightly from the true north of the sheet and varies with place and time.
One of the four main directions, north, south, east and west.
One of the four directions lying between the cardinal points, the north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.

items: In the Northern Hemisphere the pole star stands almost above the north point of the sky, so the direction of the pole star gives the north.
The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so the direction of the rising or setting sun gives the line of east and west, and the north lies at right angles to that line.

With a watch, hold it horizontally and point the hour hand at the sun; the bisector of the angle between the hour hand and the twelve mark points north in the Northern Hemisphere and south in the Southern Hemisphere.
A magnetic compass gives the magnetic north, and the variation between the magnetic north and the true north must be allowed for on a large-scale map.

learn.title: Scale and the measurement of distance

blocks.text: The scale of a map is the ratio between the distance on the map and the corresponding distance on the ground. It is expressed in three ways. The representative fraction writes the ratio as one number over another, and the denominator is the number of map units that represent one unit on the ground, so 1:50,000 means that one centimetre on the map is fifty thousand centimetres, that is five hundred metres or half a kilometre, on the ground. The statement of scale says the same thing in words, as '2 cm represents 1 km'. The graphic scale is a bar drawn on the map and divided into equal parts, each part standing for a known ground distance, and it is measured with the same ruler and in the same way as the distance that is being measured, so that the enlargement of the printed map makes no difference. The scale of a map is chosen to suit the purpose: a large scale, such as 1:2,500 or 1:25,000, shows a small area in great detail and is used for a town guide map or a cadastral map, while a small scale, such as 1:5,000,000, shows the whole of a country and is used for an atlas or a wall map.

blocks.caption: Table: converting a scale from one form to another
columns: What 1 cm on the map represents

items: To convert a representative fraction into a statement of scale, multiply the denominator by the unit on the map and then write the result in the largest convenient unit.
To convert a statement of scale into a representative fraction, write the ground distance in the same unit as the map distance, so '2 cm represents 1 km' becomes 1:50,000.
On a winding road the distance is measured in short straight steps with the divider, following the bends of the road, and the total is read off the graphic scale.
For a straight line between two points the distance is measured with a ruler, and if the map is not to scale in that direction the paper must be allowed for, as it shrinks in the heat.
A large scale shows more detail, such as the individual buildings of a town, while a small scale shows the general pattern of a region.

blocks.text: Every topographical sheet and every town guide map is ruled with a grid of straight lines so that the position of any feature can be stated exactly and not merely described. On the national grid of the Survey of India the lines running east to west are the northings and the lines running north to south are the eastings. The lines are numbered from the origin of the grid, and the origin is placed so that no part of the sheet carries a negative number. To give the grid reference of a point, the easting is read first and the northing second, and each is written as two figures, so the reference of a point is written as four figures. The point is found by running along the grid line of the easting to the grid line of the northing and noting the two numbers. If the point falls in the middle of a square rather than on a line, the extra digit that is needed is taken from the line that is nearest to the point in the direction in which it is measured, and the reference then has six figures. On a large-scale map of a town the grid of the map is often lettered in the squares, as in a chessboard, and the reference is then a letter and a number, such as B2.

items: The four-figure grid reference of a point is the easting first and the northing second, and it is always written without any gap between them.
A six-figure grid reference is used when the exact position inside the square matters, and the extra digit is taken from the nearer line.
On a map of a small town the squares are often lettered, and the reference of a feature is then given by its letter and number, such as C4.
Latitude and longitude are the coordinates used on the world map and on the maps of a whole country, and they are explained in the chapter on the geographic grid.
A location on a map should always be given by the grid reference and not by the name of the place alone, because the name may be written at some distance from the feature itself.

blocks.text: A contour line is a line on a map joining points that are at the same height above mean sea level. The lines are drawn at a fixed vertical distance apart, and this distance is the contour interval, which is printed on the sheet. The chief use of the contours is to show the shape, or relief, of the land, because the spacing and the shape of the lines carry the information: the closer the lines are to one another, the steeper the slope, and the wider apart they are, the gentler the slope. A closed set of concentric contours with the values rising towards the centre marks a hill, and a conical hill is one whose contours are evenly spaced and nearly circular. A set of contours forming a V with the point of the V towards the higher ground marks a valley, because the contour lines bend upstream as they cross the valley. A U-shaped pattern with the closed end towards the high ground and the open end downhill marks a spur or ridge, and the opposite pattern, the re-entrant, marks a small valley cut into a hillside. A flat-topped hill, with contours close together at the edges and none inside, is a plateau. Contours that are crowded together at the top and spread out below, ending in a cliff line, mark an escarpment, and the same crowding where the land falls to the shore marks a sea cliff. Where two hills meet and the contours of the two run together in a figure of eight, the low point between them is a saddle or col.

rows: Closed concentric contours with the values rising towards the centre
A hill, and a conical hill when the spacing is even

A valley, because the contours bend upstream

A flat area enclosed by contours with none inside it

A saddle or a col between two hills

items: A gentle slope is shown by widely spaced contours, and a steep slope by contours that are close together.
A uniform slope is one on which the contours are evenly spaced all the way up.
The direction of a river on the map can be found from the contours, because the V of the contours points upstream, that is, towards the higher ground.
A cliff is shown by a set of contours very close together, or by two or more contours that actually run into one another.

blocks.text: Beyond the relief, a map is read for the pattern of the settlement, the lines of communication and the drainage. Settlement is nucleated where the people of a district gather round a market, a temple, a fort or a crossing of a river, and it is dispersed where the land is broken up and the people live on their own holdings; a line of settlement along a road, a river or the coast is a linear or ribbon settlement, and it is common in the foothills and along the banks of the Ganga and the Punjab rivers. Roads follow the relief, for a road avoids a steep slope and a swamp and keeps to the gentler ground, and the trunk roads of a district therefore show the shape of the land well. In the pattern of the rivers, a dendritic pattern, like the branches of a tree, is the normal pattern over gently sloping rock, while a radial pattern, in which the streams run outwards in all directions from a central high ground, is found on a dome or a volcanic cone.

items: A dense cluster of buildings marks a nucleated settlement, and scattered buildings over the fields mark a dispersed one.
The roads that radiate from a town towards the villages around it show a star-shaped road pattern, and the roads that follow the edge of a river or a scarp follow the line of the feature.
A reservoir or a tank may be used for the storage of water for irrigation and for the town, and a canal carries the water from one river to another.
A place where a road crosses a river by a bridge is a natural crossing point, and such places often grow into towns.

keyPoints: A conventional sign is a symbol agreed upon for a feature, and the key of the map lists them all.
On a topographical sheet blue marks the water, green the vegetation, brown the contours and relief, black the buildings and the lettering, and yellow the roads.
The cardinal points are north, south, east and west, and the intercardinal points are north-east, south-east, south-west and north-west.
A three-figure bearing is measured clockwise from north, so north is 000 degrees and south-west is 225 degrees.
The bearing of a place from another place and the bearing of the second from the first differ by 180 degrees.
A scale is written as a representative fraction, as a statement of scale or as a graphic scale.
In 1:50,000 one centimetre on the map represents half a kilometre on the ground.
The graphic scale is measured with the same ruler and in the same way as the distance on the map.
A large scale shows a small area in detail and a small scale shows a wide area in general.
On the national grid the easting is read first and the northing second, and a four-figure reference is written without a gap.
The contour interval is the vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines.
Close contours show a steep slope and wide contours show a gentle slope.
The V of the contours points upstream, so the direction of a river is read from the shape of the contours.
Concentric contours mark a hill, a U opening downhill a ridge, and contours crowded above a cliff line an escarpment.
The map work record file carries 10 marks and the project report 10 marks within the internal assessment.
examFocus: A map work question is read in three steps: read the key, fix the direction and the scale, and then read the contours for the relief.
Before answering any question on a map, state the scale and the direction in which north lies, because almost every answer depends on them.
For a question on the scale, show the working, such as 6 cm multiplied by 0.5 km for a scale of 1:50,000, and remember to write the unit.
For a contour question, quote the pattern that you can see, such as the V of the contours pointing uphill, and then name the feature, so that the marks are earned twice over.
For a sketch map, remember the four things that every map must show: a title, a north arrow, a scale and a key, together with the labels of the places.
A grid reference is always written easting first, so read the number from the side and then from the bottom.

vocabulary.meaning: A symbol agreed upon and used on a map to show a particular feature.
The panel of a map that lists its symbols and their meanings.
The setting out of the map with north at the top.
The direction of a line measured clockwise from north and written in degrees.
The scale written as a ratio, such as 1:50,000.
A divided bar on the map that shows the ground distance of each of its divisions.
A line joining points that are at the same height above mean sea level.
The vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines.
The number of the easting and the northing that fix the position of a point on a map.
A permanent mark of known height above mean sea level, shown by a circle with a dot at the centre.

questions.prompt: On a topographical sheet, the colour used to show rivers, tanks and the sea is:
questions.explanation: Blue is the colour of water on a topographical sheet. Green shows the vegetation, brown the contours and the relief, and yellow the roads.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing green, which shows the forests and orchards.

questions.prompt: The three-figure bearing of south-west is:
questions.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, so north is 000°, north-east is 045°, east is 090°, south-east is 135°, south is 180°, south-west is 225° and west is 270°.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 045°, which is the bearing of the north-east, the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: On a map of 1:50,000, one centimetre represents:
questions.explanation: The denominator is the number of centimetres on the map that stand for one centimetre on the ground, so 50,000 cm is 500 m, that is half a kilometre.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing 50 m, which would be the scale of 1:5,000 and not of 1:50,000.

questions.prompt: The contour pattern that shows a spur or a ridge is:
options: A U shape with the closed end towards the high ground and the open end downhill
A V shape with the point of the V towards the higher ground
Concentric closed contours with the values rising towards the centre
Contours very close together all round
questions.answer: A U shape with the closed end towards the high ground and the open end downhill
questions.explanation: A spur or ridge projects from the high ground, so its contours form a U with the closed end uphill and the open end downhill. A V with the point uphill is a valley, and concentric closed contours mark a hill.
questions.commonMistake: Choosing the V shape, which is the pattern of a valley, where the contours bend upstream.

questions.prompt: On the national grid, the four-figure grid reference of a point is read:
options: Both from the bottom of the sheet
Both from the left of the sheet
questions.explanation: The easting is the vertical line and is read from the left, and the northing is the horizontal line and is read from the bottom. The two figures are written together without a gap.
questions.commonMistake: Reading the northing first, which reverses the reference and places the point in the wrong square.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines is called the contour ______.
questions.explanation: The contour interval is the vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines, and it is printed on the sheet so that the height of any point on a contour can be worked out.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'line', which names the contour itself rather than the distance between contours.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a scale expressed as 1:50,000 is called a representative ______.
questions.explanation: The representative fraction writes the scale as a ratio of two numbers, and the other two forms are the statement of scale and the graphic scale.
questions.commonMistake: Answering 'scale', which names all three forms together rather than the ratio.

questions.prompt: State two ways of finding the north direction on the ground without the use of a compass, and explain how each works.
questions.answer: Using the pole star: in the Northern Hemisphere the pole star stands almost exactly above the north point of the sky, and it can be picked out among the stars of the Plough or the Big Dipper, whose two end stars point towards it. The direction in which it is seen is therefore the direction of north. Using the sun: the sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so the direction in which the sun rises or sets gives the line of east and west; the north is then found at right angles to that line, on the side of the pole star. A third method uses a watch: it is held horizontally with the hour hand pointing at the sun, and the bisector of the angle between the hour hand and the twelve mark gives the north in the Northern Hemisphere, because the watch runs at half the rate of the sun.
questions.explanation: Each method has to be explained, because the marks are for the reason and not only for the name.
questions.commonMistake: Writing only that the pole star indicates north without saying that it stands above the north point of the sky.

questions.prompt: A map is drawn to a scale of 1:25,000. (a) Write the scale as a statement of scale. (b) What distance on the ground is represented by 4 cm on the map? (c) Give the scale of the same map in the form of a graphic scale description.
questions.answer: In the representative fraction 1:25,000, one unit on the map stands for 25,000 of the same units on the ground, so one centimetre stands for 25,000 cm, which is 250 metres. Therefore the statement of scale is: 1 cm represents 250 m, or equivalently 4 cm represents 1 km. For 4 cm on the map, the ground distance is 4 multiplied by 250 m, which is 1,000 m, that is 1 kilometre. As a graphic scale the bar is drawn with divisions of a convenient length, for example each division of 2 cm on the map may stand for 500 m on the ground and the bar is labelled 0, 500 m, 1 km, 1.5 km and so on, so that a distance measured on the map with a ruler is read off the bar and converted into the ground distance.
questions.explanation: The conversion has to be worked through and the units written at each step.
questions.commonMistake: Giving 1,000 m without converting it to 1 km, or writing the statement of scale as 1 cm represents 25 km.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would find the distance between two places on a road on a topographical map, and state two points to be careful about.
questions.answer: First read the scale of the sheet and identify the graphic scale bar. Then place one end of the graphic scale bar on the first place and move the bar along the road, keeping it on the road, until the other end of the bar reaches the second place, turning the bar at each bend. Count the number of divisions of the bar that have been used and multiply that number by the ground distance of one division, which is written on the bar. Two points must be remembered. The distance must be measured along the road and not as a straight line between the two places, because the road may wind round a hill or follow a valley, and the straight line would give a distance that is too short. The map itself may have shrunk after printing, so the bar and the distance must be measured with the same ruler and in the same way, and for very long distances along a winding road the measurement is made in short straight steps with a pair of dividers rather than in one long placement of the bar.
questions.explanation: The method, the reading of the bar and the two cautions all have to be there.
questions.commonMistake: Measuring the straight line between the two places instead of the distance along the road.

questions.prompt: Describe the features shown by the contours of a topographical map, and explain how a map is used to show the relief of the land.
questions.answer: A contour line is a line drawn on a map joining all the points that are at the same height above mean sea level. The lines are drawn at a constant vertical distance apart, and that distance is the contour interval, which is printed on the sheet. The contours are the means by which the shape of the land, or the relief, is shown on a flat sheet. The first thing they show is the slope. Where the contour lines are close together the ground rises quickly, and where they are far apart it rises gently, and a slope on which the spacing is the same all the way is a uniform slope. The second thing they show is the form of the land. A set of closed concentric contours with the values rising towards the centre marks a hill, and a hill whose contours are evenly spaced and nearly circular is a conical hill. A flat-topped hill, in which the contours are crowded at the edges and there are none inside, is a plateau. Contours that are crowded together at the top and spread out below, ending in a cliff line, mark an escarpment, and where the land falls sheer to the shore the crowding of the contours marks a sea cliff. A U-shaped pattern with the closed end towards the high ground and the open end downhill marks a spur or a ridge, and the opposite pattern is a re-entrant, a small valley cut into the hillside. Where the contours of two hills run together in a figure of eight the low point between them is a saddle. The third thing the contours show is the drainage, because the contour lines bend into a V as they cross a valley, and the point of the V points upstream, so the flow of the river can be read from the map. Relief also helps in other ways, since a road avoids a steep slope and a settlement grows in a sheltered plain, so the pattern of the roads and of the villages on the map is largely a pattern of the relief beneath them.
questions.explanation: The definition and the contour interval come first, then the three things the contours show, and each has to be illustrated.
questions.commonMistake: Saying that a V pointing upstream marks a ridge, when the V of a valley always points towards the higher ground.

questions.prompt: What is a conventional sign? Explain how the colours of a topographical sheet are used, and state what a reader should do before answering any question on a map.
questions.answer: A conventional sign is a symbol that has been agreed upon and used on the maps of a country to show a particular feature, so that it can be recognised at once. The list of the signs with their meanings is printed on the map in the key, or legend, and the signs are designed to suggest the feature, so that a railway line is drawn as a line with short bars across it like the sleepers of a track, a bridge as two short parallel lines across the road or the stream, a church as a cross, a mosque as a small dome with a minaret, and a lighthouse as a tower with rays drawn from the top. The colours are used in the same systematic way. Blue marks the water, so that rivers, streams, canals and tanks are picked out at once. Green marks the vegetation, the forests, the scrub and the orchards. Brown marks the contours and the relief, and also the roads in cutting and embankment. Black is used for the buildings, the lettering and the railways. Yellow is used for the roads, with a red band for the national highways and a white band for the metalled roads, and red is used for the built-up area of a town on a political map. Before answering any question on a map the reader must first read the key, because the meaning of a symbol can differ from one map to another and the key is the only place where it is stated. The reader must then note the scale of the sheet and the direction in which north lies, because most of the answers depend on them, and if the map carries a grid, the grid reference of the feature asked about should be noted so that the answer is tied to a position on the sheet. Only then is the map read for the particular information that the question requires.
questions.explanation: The definition, the system of the colours and the reading routine at the end all have to be present.
questions.commonMistake: Leaving out the last part, that the key must be read before anything else, which is the point of the question.

questions.prompt: A student says that a topographical sheet is only a picture of the ground, and that a person who cannot draw well will do badly in map work. Examine this claim and show what map work really requires of a student.
questions.answer: The claim mistakes the map for a picture and understates what map work asks for. A topographical sheet is not a picture, for it is built on conventions that have to be read. It is a set of agreed signs, a scale, an orientation and a set of lines, and everything that the sheet says has to be read through those conventions rather than seen. A reader who knows that a blue line is a river, that brown lines are contours of a fixed interval, that a yellow band with a red border is a trunk road, that north is at the top, that the denominator of the scale gives the ground distance, and that a V in the contours points upstream, can extract a great deal from a sheet. A reader who cannot draw will still read all of that, because the reading of a map depends on recognising the conventions and reasoning from them rather than on the ability to reproduce a picture. It is true that one exercise in the record file, the sketch map, asks for a drawing, and there the skill that is needed is not artistic but orderly: the student has to decide what to show, where to put it and how to label it, and the standard is that the sketch map carries a title, a north arrow, a scale and a key, that the positions are roughly correct in relation to one another and that the routes are clear. A neat diagram that is wrongly oriented is worse than a rough one that is right. It is also worth noticing that the map work is not a test of drawing at all but of the five conventions, and that the same skill carries into the rest of the paper, because a candidate who can read the scale, the direction and the contours of a map can answer the interpretation questions of the theory paper as well. So the claim is true only in the narrowest sense that one exercise needs a sketch; it is false as a general judgement, and the preparation that matters is the learning of the conventions and the practice of reading them.
questions.explanation: The answer has to take the claim apart, show what the map really is, and then show what skill the map work actually tests.
questions.commonMistake: Agreeing that map work is a test of drawing, which misses the point that the drawing is only one exercise of the six.

assessment.title: Map Work Assessment
instructions: These exercises stand for the record file of the map work that the internal assessment asks for. Work through each exercise with the data printed with it.
Every exercise below is given as text and tables, so no map sheet is needed; the data given with an exercise is the whole of the information on which the answer depends.
Read the scale and the direction of north before you answer anything, and show the working for every calculation of distance.
For the contour exercises, describe the pattern of the lines that you can see and then name the feature, so that the reason is given as well as the answer.
The answer key is given with each exercise under the 'Show answer key' tab. Read the explanation as well as the answer, because the explanation is where the marks are earned.
This exercise set is original practice written for BoardPrep. It is not a previous year paper and it is not a survey sheet issued by the Survey of India.

exercises.prompt: For each of the five map extracts described below, name the type of the map and state one use of that type of map.

table.caption: Table: the five map extracts
rows: A map of India on which the rainfall is printed in millimetres in different shades
A single sheet of a town and the country around it, on which the roads, the railways, the buildings, the rivers and the contours are all shown
A booklet of maps, one for each state of India, showing the boundaries, the cities and the main roads
A sheet of a village on which every plot of land is marked out and the name of its owner is written on it
A map of India published in a newspaper on which the rainfall of the past week is shown by lines called isobars

exercises.answer: A: A thematic map, specifically an isohyet map, used to show the distribution of rainfall over an area. B: A topographical map, used to study the relief, drainage, settlement and lines of communication of an area. C: An atlas map, used for reference and for finding the position of a place. D: A cadastral map, or village land record map, used to show the boundaries and the ownership of land. E: A weather map, used to follow the weather and to give warning of storms.
exercises.explanation: The type is decided by what the map shows rather than by its size. A is thematic because one particular element, the rainfall, is plotted over the whole country; B is topographical because the whole range of physical and human features is shown on one sheet at a large scale; C is an atlas because it is a collection of maps in a book; D is cadastral because it records the boundaries and the ownership of plots; and E is a weather map because the isobars show the pressure pattern of the period. Once the type is named, the use follows from it, and the uses in the answer are the ones the syllabus links with each type.

exercises.prompt: The extract below is a town guide map with north at the top of the sheet. (a) State two ways of finding north on the ground without using a compass. (b) Using the grid squares given, state the direction from the railway station to the church, and from the church to the post office. (c) Give the three-figure bearing of the railway station as seen from the church.

data.label: Railway station
data.value: Grid square B2

data.label: Church
data.value: Grid square D1

data.label: Post office
data.value: Grid square A4

data.label: Footbridge over the river
data.value: Grid square C3

exercises.answer: (a) The pole star stands almost above the north point of the sky, so the direction in which it is seen gives the north. The sun rises in the east and sets in the west, so the direction of the rising or setting sun gives the line of east and west, and the north is at right angles to it. (b) From the railway station at B2 to the church at D1 the direction is north-east, because D1 lies north and east of B2. From the church at D1 to the post office at A4 the direction is south-west, because A4 lies south and west of D1. (c) The three-figure bearing of the railway station from the church is 225°.
exercises.explanation: The grid of the sheet runs north to south and east to west, so the direction from one square to another is found by asking which way the second square lies in each of the two directions. The church at D1 is north-east of the station at B2, so the station seen from the church is to the south-west, and a bearing measured clockwise from north gives south-west as 180° plus 45°, which is 225°. Note that the bearing from the station to the church is the opposite, 045°.

exercises.prompt: The extract is printed to a representative fraction of 1:50,000, and on the printed sheet the distance from the railway bridge to the post office measures 6 cm. The graphic scale bar shows that each division of 4 cm on the map stands for 2 km on the ground. (a) Write the scale of the map as a statement of scale. (b) Find the actual distance in kilometres between the railway bridge and the post office. (c) Explain in one or two sentences how a graphic scale is used to measure a distance on a map.

data.label: Measured distance on the sheet
data.value: 6 cm

data.label: Graphic scale bar
data.value: Each division of 4 cm on the map stands for 2 km on the ground

exercises.answer: (a) 1 cm represents 500 m on the ground, or 2 cm represents 1 km. (b) 3 km. Using the representative fraction, 6 cm multiplied by 500 m gives 3,000 m, which is 3 km. Using the graphic scale, 6 cm is one and a half divisions of the bar, and one and a half multiplied by 2 km also gives 3 km. (c) The graphic scale is a bar divided into equal parts, each part showing a known ground distance, and the bar is measured with the same ruler and in the same way as the distance being measured, so that the number of divisions used is multiplied by the ground distance of one division.
exercises.explanation: In the representative fraction the denominator is the number of centimetres on the map that stand for one centimetre on the ground, so 50,000 cm is 500 m, and 6 cm therefore stands for 3,000 m. The two methods give the same answer, which is the check that the reading of the scale is correct. In the last part the point to make is that the bar and the map are measured in the same way, so that a shrinking of the printed sheet does not affect the answer.

exercises.prompt: The key of the town guide map of a town is given below. (a) Which colour shows a forest on this map? (b) Which symbol shows a railway line? (c) Which symbol shows a bridge? (d) Which symbol shows a church? (e) Which symbol shows a benchmark, and what does the number beside it give? (f) State how you would measure the distance from the bus stand to the library along the road on this map.

table.caption: Table: the key of the town guide map
columns: Symbol or colour on the map
rows: A black line with short cross bars
A yellow band with a red border
Two short parallel lines drawn across a road or a stream
A small circle with a dot at the centre
A tower with rays drawn from the top

exercises.answer: (a) A forest is shown in green. (b) A railway line is shown by a black line with short cross bars across it, like the sleepers of a track. (c) A bridge is shown by two short parallel lines drawn across the road or the stream. (d) A church is shown by a small cross. (e) A benchmark is shown by a small circle with a dot at the centre, and the number beside it gives the height of that point above mean sea level in metres. (f) The graphic scale bar of the map is placed with one end on the bus stand, moved along the road to the library, and the number of divisions of the bar that have been used is multiplied by the ground distance of one division, so that the length of the road is converted into the real distance.
exercises.explanation: Every answer is read straight from the key, which is the point of the exercise, and the last answer tests the method of measuring a distance along a road. The distance is measured along the road and not as a straight line between the two places, because the road may bend.

exercises.prompt: The patterns of the contour lines described below are taken from a topographical sheet. (a) Name the relief feature shown by each of the six patterns. (b) State how a steep slope and a gentle slope are shown by the contours, and how a uniform slope is shown. (c) What is the contour interval, and how is it shown on the sheet?

data.label: Pattern 1
data.value: A set of closed concentric contours with the values rising towards the centre

data.label: Pattern 2
data.value: Contours that form a V with the point of the V towards the higher ground

data.label: Pattern 3
data.value: Contours that form a U with the closed end towards the higher ground and the open end downhill

data.label: Pattern 4
data.value: A large flat area enclosed by contours, with no contours inside it

data.label: Pattern 5
data.value: Contours very close together at the top and far apart at the bottom, with the lowest contour ending in a cliff line

data.label: Pattern 6
data.value: Contours very close together where the land falls straight down to the shore

exercises.answer: (a) 1: A hill, and a conical hill where the contours are evenly spaced and nearly circular. 2: A valley, because the contours bend upstream as they cross it. 3: A spur or a ridge, which projects from the higher ground. 4: A plateau. 5: An escarpment. 6: A sea cliff. (b) A steep slope is shown by contour lines that are close together, and a gentle slope by lines that are far apart; a uniform slope is one on which the spacing of the contours is the same at every level. (c) The contour interval is the vertical distance between two consecutive contour lines, and it is printed on the sheet, usually in a corner, so that the height of any point on a contour can be worked out.
exercises.explanation: The reason is in the shape of the lines, and the answer should quote it. Pattern 2 is a valley because the contour lines bend into a V as they cross a valley and the point of the V points upstream, that is, towards the higher ground. Pattern 3 is the opposite, a spur or ridge projecting downhill, with the closed end of the U uphill. Pattern 5 is an escarpment because the land falls in a single steep step, and pattern 6 is a sea cliff because the fall is sheer to the water.

exercises.prompt: You have to draw a sketch map to organise the information about a visit to the city zoo. The layout is given below. (a) State the four things that every sketch map must show besides the information itself. (b) State the direction of each of the first five places from the main gate. (c) Give one reason why a sketch map is used in place of a photograph of the zoo.

data.label: Main entrance gate
data.value: On the southern side of the zoo

data.label: Lion enclosure
data.value: North-east of the gate

data.label: Elephant enclosure
data.value: Due east of the gate

data.label: Children's park
data.value: North-west of the gate

data.label: Reptile house
data.value: South-east of the gate

data.label: Office of the curator
data.value: Due north of the gate

data.label: Canteen
data.value: On the western side, opposite the children's park

data.label: Zoo hospital
data.value: Next to the office of the curator

exercises.answer: (a) The four things are a title, a north arrow or an indication of direction, a scale, and a key or legend, together with the clear labels of the places shown. (b) The lion enclosure lies to the north-east of the gate, the elephant enclosure to the east, the children's park to the north-west, the reptile house to the south-east, and the office of the curator to the north. The canteen lies to the west and the zoo hospital to the north, next to the curator's office. (c) A sketch map shows the relative position of the places and the routes between them clearly and simply, and it can be drawn quickly with the few details that matter, whereas a photograph does not show the layout of the zoo, the directions of the places or the distances between them.
exercises.explanation: The four items in part (a) are the standard requirements of any map and they are the marks for that part. In part (b) the directions are read straight from the information given, and the answer should be read from the gate, since that is the point of observation. In part (c) the reason must be about the information a map gives and a photograph does not.
